name: Numbers
v: The day Moses finished setting up the tabernacle, he anointed it and consecrated it — every part of it, every tool, the altar and all its gear. He anointed them and set them apart as holy.
Then the leaders of Israel stepped forward — the heads of their fathers' houses, the chiefs of the tribes, the men who had overseen the census.
They brought their offering before the LORD: six covered wagons and twelve oxen — a wagon for every two leaders, an ox for each one — and they presented them in front of the tabernacle.
The LORD said to Moses,
"Take them. Use them for the work of the tent of meeting. Distribute them to the Levites — each according to what his service requires."
So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites.
To the sons of Gershon he gave two wagons and four oxen — what their service required.
To the sons of Merari he gave four wagons and eight oxen — what their service required, under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest.
To the sons of Kohath he gave nothing. Their charge was the holy things, which they had to carry on their shoulders.
On the day the altar was anointed, the leaders brought their dedication offerings and set them before the altar.
The LORD said to Moses, "One leader per day. Each one will present his offering for the dedication of the altar."
Day one — Nahshon son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah.
His offering: a silver platter weighing 130 shekels, a silver bowl of 70 shekels by the sanctuary standard, both heaped with fine flour mixed with oil for the grain offering;
a gold dish of 10 shekels filled with incense;
a young bull, a ram, and a year-old lamb for the burnt offering;
a male goat for the sin offering;
and for the peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five male goats, five year-old lambs. That was Nahshon's offering.
Day two — Nethanel son of Zuar, leader of Issachar.
He brought: a silver platter of 130 shekels, a silver bowl of 70 by the sanctuary standard, both filled with flour mixed with oil for the grain offering;
a gold dish of 10 shekels full of incense;
a young bull, a ram, a year-old lamb for the burnt offering;
a male goat for sin;
and for peace — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. That was Nethanel's offering.
Day three — Eliab son of Helon, leader of Zebulun.
His offering: a silver platter of 130 shekels, a silver bowl of 70 by the sanctuary standard, both filled with flour and oil for grain;
a gold dish of 10 shekels of incense;
a young bull, a ram, a year-old lamb for burnt offering;
a male goat for sin;
for peace — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five lambs a year old. Eliab's offering.
Day four — Elizur son of Shedeur, leader of Reuben.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — both full of flour and oil for grain;
gold dish of 10 shekels, incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Elizur's offering.
Day five — Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai, leader of Simeon.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — both full of flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels, incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Shelumiel's offering.
Day six — Eliasaph son of Deuel, leader of Gad.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels of incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Eliasaph's offering.
Day seven — Elishama son of Ammihud, leader of Ephraim.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — both filled with flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels, incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Elishama's offering.
Day eight — Gamaliel son of Pedahzur, leader of Manasseh.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels of incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Gamaliel's offering.
Day nine — Abidan son of Gideoni, leader of Benjamin.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels, incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Abidan's offering.
Day ten — Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai, leader of Dan.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels of incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Ahiezer's offering.
Day eleven — Pagiel son of Ochran, leader of Asher.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels, incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Pagiel's offering.
Day twelve — Ahira son of Enan, leader of Naphtali.
His offering: silver platter, 130 shekels; silver bowl, 70 — flour and oil for grain;
gold dish, 10 shekels of incense;
young bull, ram, year-old lamb — burnt offering;
male goat — sin offering;
peace offering — two oxen, five rams, five goats, five year-old lambs. Ahira's offering.
This was the dedication of the altar from the leaders of Israel on the day it was anointed: twelve silver platters, twelve silver bowls, twelve gold dishes.
Each platter, 130 shekels of silver; each bowl, 70. Total silver from the vessels — 2,400 shekels by the sanctuary standard.
The twelve gold dishes filled with incense — 10 shekels apiece by the sanctuary standard. Total gold: 120 shekels.
All the animals for the burnt offering: twelve bulls, twelve rams, twelve year-old lambs, with their grain offerings; twelve male goats for the sin offering.
For the peace offering: twenty-four oxen, sixty rams, sixty male goats, sixty year-old lambs. That was the dedication of the altar after it was anointed.

And when Moses entered the tent of meeting to speak with him, he heard the voice — speaking to him from above the atonement cover on the ark of the testimony, between the two cherubim. That was how he spoke to him.

com.d:
# Numbers 7: The Grace of Ordered Giving

The spiritual heart of Numbers 7 beats with a profound truth: God receives the gifts of His people with meticulous care and delight, treating each offering with equal weight and significance. This lengthy chapter, which catalogs the nearly identical donations of twelve tribal leaders, reveals that worship is dignified not by uniqueness but by sincere, ordered participation in community.

When the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribal leader brought identical offerings—a silver plate, a silver bowl, a gold dish, animals for sacrifice, and grain offerings. Rather than condense this repetition, the text honors each tribe by recording their gifts in full. This remarkable repetition teaches us something vital: God is not bored by faithfulness. He does not skim the second and third accounts to get to the punchline. Each offering matters. Each giver matters. The symmetry itself communicates that all God's people have equal standing before Him, whether they lead a large tribe or a small one.

This has immediate application to our own church communities. We live in a culture that prizes novelty and distinction, where only the unusual makes headlines. Yet Numbers 7 suggests that faithful, consistent participation in the ordinary rhythms of worship—the weekly giving, the weekly gathering, the weekly commitment—constitutes a profound spiritual beauty. The banker who quietly tithes alongside the entrepreneur; the homemaker serving in Sunday school alongside the executive; the single adult giving faithfully alongside the family—all are recorded in heaven's registry with the same sacred attention the Levites gave to each tribal leader's gift.

The practical challenge is refusing to measure our spiritual significance by visibility or impact. God is building His kingdom through countless acts of ordinary faithfulness, each one valued as highly as any dramatic gesture. Where have you been tempted to think your faithful giving, your presence, your service doesn't matter because it's not remarkable? What would change if you believed God treasures it exactly as He treasured those twelve identical offerings?
com.s:
Numbers 7 constitutes the longest chapter in the Pentateuch, comprising eighty-nine verses that meticulously document the dedicatory offerings presented by the tribal leaders of Israel for the newly consecrated tabernacle. This material belongs to the Priestly source and follows directly upon the completion of the tabernacle's erection and anointing described in the preceding chapters. The temporal notice in verse 1, linking these events to the day Moses finished setting up the tabernacle, creates an important chronological connection to Exodus 40, though the relationship between this date and the census of Numbers 1 has occasioned scholarly discussion regarding the compositional history of these opening chapters.

The chapter's most striking literary feature is its extensive repetition, as each of the twelve tribal leaders presents identical offerings over twelve consecutive days. This repetitive structure, while seeming redundant to modern readers, serves significant theological and rhetorical purposes within ancient Near Eastern dedicatory contexts. The Hebrew term *nāśîʾ* (prince, chieftain) designates these tribal heads, the same leaders enumerated in Numbers 1:5–16 who assisted Moses with the census. Their role here demonstrates that Israel's worship involves the entire community through its representative leadership.

The offerings themselves include silver vessels measured by the sanctuary shekel (*šeqel haqqōdeš*), terminology indicating a standardized weight system maintained at the central sanctuary. The presentation of wagons and oxen for transporting the tabernacle furnishings reflects practical liturgical concerns, with the Levitical clans receiving allocations proportional to their assigned burdens. Notably, the Kohathites receive no wagons because they must carry the most sacred objects upon their shoulders.

The chapter concludes with a remarkable theophanic notice: Moses enters the tent of meeting and hears the divine voice speaking from above the *kappōret* (mercy seat) between the cherubim. This detail connects the elaborate dedicatory ritual to its ultimate purpose—establishing the locus of divine-human communication. Some interpreters view this conclusion as the literary and theological climax toward which the entire chapter builds, demonstrating that authentic worship, properly offered through designated channels, creates the conditions for ongoing divine revelation. The passage thus bridges the completion of sacred space with its functional purpose as the site of theophanic encounter.
com.p:
Numbers 7 stands as one of the longest chapters in all of Scripture, yet every repetitive word carries covenantal weight. This passage unfolds approximately 1,445 years before Christ, in the second year after Israel's exodus from Egypt, precisely one month after the tabernacle was erected in the wilderness of Sinai. Within the grand arc of redemption, we stand at the Exodus phase—God has delivered His people from bondage and is now constituting them as a kingdom of priests, establishing the visible dwelling of His presence among them through the tabernacle system that points forward to the Incarnation.

The twelve tribal leaders bring identical offerings over twelve consecutive days for the dedication of the altar. The meticulous repetition, far from being tedious, reveals profound prophetic truth: God sees each tribe distinctly, receives each gift personally, and records each act of worship individually. This foreshadows how Christ, the true altar upon whom all sacrifices find their fulfillment, receives the offering of every nation, tribe, and tongue with equal delight. The uniformity of the gifts points to the one sacrifice sufficient for all—the Lamb of God whose single offering perfects forever those who are sanctified.

The wagons and oxen given for transporting the tabernacle reveal God's provision for bearing His presence through the wilderness journey. The Kohathites, who carried the most holy objects on their shoulders, received no wagons—a typological indication that what is most sacred in God's economy cannot be mechanized or made convenient. Christ Himself bore the weight of our salvation upon His own shoulders, carrying the cross that would become the true mercy seat.

Moses entering the tent to hear God's voice speaking from between the cherubim above the ark anticipates the torn veil and opened access that Christ's death would accomplish. What Moses alone experienced—direct communion with the speaking God—becomes the inheritance of every believer through the mediatorial work of Christ, our greater Moses who brings us into the holy of holies.

The altar dedication required blood, grain, oil, and incense—elements pointing to Christ's sacrificial death, His perfect humanity as the bread of life, the anointing of the Spirit, and the fragrant offering of His obedience ascending to the Father. For the church dwelling between the advents, this chapter summons us to bring our offerings with equal intentionality, knowing that our worship, united to Christ's perfect offering, rises before the throne as a pleasing aroma while we await the final dedication of the New Jerusalem, where God Himself will be the temple.
